html:
Sook Ching was the mass killing of Chinese men in Singapore by the Japanese military police after the fall of Singapore in February 1942. Men were screened at centres across the island, and those picked out were taken to beaches and shot.

Japan targeted the Chinese because many had backed China against Japan. Japanese figures admitted about 5,000 deaths; Singaporean estimates run far higher, up to tens of thousands.

The massacre marked the start of three and a half years of occupation, when Singapore was renamed Syonan. It shaped the outlook of young Singaporeans such as Lee Kuan Yew, who nearly became a victim. See also Pacific War.
